text: Every lesson before this one worked in SQL. Snowpark is the piece a growing share of current Snowflake job postings ask for by name: a Python API that builds and runs real data transformations without ever pulling the data out of Snowflake. The code gets translated and pushed down to execute inside Snowflake's own engine — the same RBAC, masking policies, and warehouse billing from earlier chapters still apply, because it's still Snowflake doing the work.

That code doesn't run in a separate IDE you have to stand up yourself. Python Worksheets and Notebooks are a worksheet type built into Snowsight specifically for this — you write and run Snowpark code directly inside the Snowflake UI, and a worksheet can later be deployed as a stored procedure.

A Snowpark DataFrame can come from an existing table with session dot table, or from a raw SQL string with session dot sql — and either way, nothing runs yet. Note the Python API uses snake case, group underscore by, not Spark's camelCase groupBy, a detail worth getting right if you've seen Spark's DataFrame API before.

Filter, select, and group by read almost exactly like the SQL clauses they replace, just as Python method calls instead. Chaining five of these in a row costs nothing extra — Snowflake only ever sees and optimizes the final combined query once you actually trigger it.

That's the single most important mechanical detail here: filter, select, group_by, and agg are transformations — they only build a query plan, no SQL is sent yet. A query only actually executes when you call an action: collect, count, show, or save_as_table. Calling count and then collect on the same DataFrame runs the underlying query twice, not once, unless you explicitly cache the result.

Next lesson covers the two ways Snowpark logic becomes a reusable, callable object inside Snowflake — a user-defined function you call inside a query, and a stored procedure you call, or schedule, to run a whole piece of logic.
